Language across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Between ages 7 and 9, language development continues its steep trajectory with measurable advances across all domains, shifting from foundational competence toward increasingly sophisticated, context-sensitive deployment. Vocabulary acquisition accelerates: typical children add roughly three new base (root) words a day 1; if you count derived forms (prefixes/suffixes creating new words), the effective intake is closer to 8-12 items a day. By this stage their core lexicon averages about 6-7.5k root words (roughly  6k by the end of Grade 2 and  7k by mid-late Grade 3 2) with wide spread by experience. Age  8 is also when the child’s phonological repertoire is complete 3, 4. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

During this window, vocabulary growth becomes explicitly derivative: children start using derivational morphology (i.e forming new words by adding prefixes or suffixes to a base word) as a productive tool, parsing and composing prefixes/suffixes to infer meanings and part-of-speech shifts (happy->unhappy, govern->government), a skill that accelerates towards the end of the 7- to 9-year window and contributes substantially to the surge of new words learned during the middle-elementary years 5, 6, 7; this skill does, however, remain immature through age 9. By age eight, children also understand jokes and riddles that play on sounds (e.g "what do you call a fake noodle?" -> "an impasta") 8 and start to grasp that words can carry multiple meanings (e.g literal and psychological meaning of "cold") 9, reflecting richer semantic networks that support inference and abstract reasoning; relatedly, figurative language production emerges and accelerates between ages 7-9 10, reflecting developing metalinguistic awareness, which is a strong predictor of understanding figurative language 11, though adult-like comprehension of idioms in off-line metalinguistic tasks doesn’t emerge until years later 12. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Syntactic complexity continues its nonlinear climb: between ages 7-8, use of relative pronouns (e.g who, whom, whose, which, that, whoever) and subordinate clauses (e.g "when it rang" in "she answered the phone when it rang") increases and children start using gerunds (a verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun in a sentence, e.g "running") more frequently, while towards the end of this window, subordination increases further with more advanced conjunctions such as "meanwhile", "unless", "even if", or "although" 13. Their sentences, measured properly as T-units (a main clause plus all its subordinate material), average about 7 words 14, reflecting a broad expansion of clause chaining and embedded structure beyond the mostly coordinate/"because/so" scaffolds typical at seven.

During this window, children’s stories shift from the single-episode, locally ordered tales common at seven towards sustained, multi-episode narratives that keep a global plot in view 15, chain causes and consequences explicitly (albeit in a basic and unreliable manner 16), and deploy temporal previews and summaries 17; they also attribute protagonists’ inner states far more often to motivate actions, marking a clear step up in evaluative (i.e interpreting events as a narrator would) and causal coherence 18, 19, 20, 21 (although there appears to be a tension between evaluative comments and narrative coherence at this age, likely reflecting immature semantic working memory 19). Relatedly, their narratives show richer perspective-taking: primary-school children coordinate the "landscapes" of action and consciousness more effectively, using mental-state language to explain goals and beliefs 22. In autobiographical narration, nine-year-olds’ accounts are typically more specific, temporally ordered, and causally linked than at seven, even though the most interpretive, identity-building commentary continues to rise mainly from late childhood into adolescence 23, 24, 16.

In comprehension, nine-year-olds more reliably generate and integrate both bridging and elaborative inferences (i.e "bridging" events or "elaborating" on them with prior/world knowledge), capacities tightly tied to overall comprehension and increasingly supported by growth in vocabulary, working memory, and the ability to handle embedded clause structures 25, 26.
